## Urban Outfitters, Inc.
**1809 Walnut Street
Philadelphia, [Pennsylvania](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/united-states-and-canada/us-political-geography/pennsylvania) 19103
U.S.A.**
**Telephone: (215) 564-2313
Fax: (215) 568-1549
Web site: http://www.urbanoutfitters.com**
_Public Company
Incorporated:_ 1976
_Employees:_ 6,200
_Sales:_ $827.8 million (2005)
_Stock Exchanges:_ NASDAQ
_Ticker Symbol:_ URBN
_NAIC:_ 448140 Family Clothing Stores
Urban Outfitters, Inc., operates specialty retail stores under the Urban Outfitters, Anthropologie, and Free People banners. The company operates two business segments: the lifestyle merchandising retail segment, which oversees store operations, and a wholesale apparel business. Both Urban Outfitters and Anthropologie offer customers hip and trendy apparel and home furnishings through retail locations, catalogs, and Web sites. The first Free People store opened in 2002. The freepeople.com Web site soon followed. As of January 2005, [Urban Outfitters Inc](https://www.encyclopedia.com/social-sciences-and-law/economics-business-and-labor/businesses-and-occupations/urban-outfitters). operated 65 Anthropologie stores, two Free People retail locations, and 75 Urban Outfitter stores in the [United States](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/united-states-and-canada/us-political-geography/united-states), [Canada](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/united-states-and-canada/canadian-political-geography/canada), and the [United Kingdom](https://www.encyclopedia.com/history/modern-europe/british-and-irish-history/united-kingdom-great-britain-and-northern-ireland).

## Beginnings
Urban Outfitters was created in 1970 by two retail novices, anthropology graduate Richard Hayne and his former roommate at Lehigh University, Scott Belair. Hayne was just back from two years working with Eskimos in [Alaska](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/united-states-and-canada/us-political-geography/alaska) as a VISTA Volunteer; Belair was a second-year student at Wharton School of Business and needed a project for his entrepreneur workshop. Over beer one night, the two came up with the idea of a store for college and graduate students, selling inexpensive clothes and items for dorm rooms and apartments. Pooling $5,000, they opened the Free People Store in Philadelphia, near the campus of the [University of Pennsylvania](https://www.encyclopedia.com/social-sciences-and-law/education/colleges-us/university-pennsylvania). In a 400-square-feet store decorated with packing crates and beat-up furniture, they offered inexpensive secondhand clothing, Indian fabrics, scented candles, T-shirts, drug paraphernalia, and ethnic jewelry. "I was that market," Hayne told Dan Shaw of _The [New York](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/united-states-and-canada/us-political-geography/new-york) Times_ in 1994, adding that "Everyone associated with the store was that market."
The store was a success. "Belair got an A on the project," according to Robert La Franco in a _Forbes_ article, "and went on to [Wall Street](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/united-states-and-canada/us-physical-geography/wall-street), where he started his own bankruptcy workout business." Hayne stayed with the business, adding such merchandise as coffee mugs and glassware to the product line. In 1976, he moved to larger quarters near the university, changed the store's name to Urban Outfitters, and incorporated the company. In 1980, with sales around $3 million, Hayne opened a second store, in Cambridge, [Massachusetts](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/united-states-and-canada/us-political-geography/massachusetts), close to several colleges.

## Beginnings
In 1987, Hayne hired Kenneth Cleeland as chief financial officer. Cleeland, a graduate of [George Washington](https://www.encyclopedia.com/people/history/us-history-biographies/george-washington) University, had held financial positions with several wholesale and retail companies. At Urban Outfitters, he instituted financial controls to deal with shoplifting problems and Hayne's rather casual bookkeeping practices. Profits increased, and Cleeland helped Hayne borrow $3 million to open six new stores within three years.
New stores in the chain followed the original concept and were located in metropolitan areas near college students. By 1995, Urban Outfitters stores would be established in Madison, [Wisconsin](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/united-states-and-canada/us-political-geography/wisconsin); [Ann Arbor](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/united-states-and-canada/us-political-geography/ann-arbor), [Michigan](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/united-states-and-canada/us-political-geography/michigan); Boston; [Minneapolis](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/united-states-and-canada/us-political-geography/minneapolis); [Seattle](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/united-states-and-canada/us-political-geography/seattle); [New York](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/united-states-and-canada/us-political-geography/new-york); Washington, D.C.; [Chicago](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/united-states-and-canada/us-political-geography/chicago); and Portland, Oregon. Moreover, the chain would also secure a presence in [California](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/united-states-and-canada/us-political-geography/california), with five locations in college towns. Even when Hayne was tempted to drift from his original concept, store locations kept the company focused on its college-age market.

## Beginnings
The new stores maintained Hayne's "counterculture" approach, and the company relied heavily on its buildings and interior displays to entice customers to enter, explore its stores, and buy its goods. "We always use renovated buildings," Hayne told the _Washington Post_ in a 1993 feature. "Other stores will go into a mall and put their image into a space, where we use an existing space to enhance our image. None of our stores look alike. We go into these old buildings and adapt them for ourselves," he noted. In Washington, D.C., for example, the company took over a Woolworth's store, complete with worn wooden floors, exposed brick walls, and a steel staircase to the basement. The [Ann Arbor](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/united-states-and-canada/us-political-geography/ann-arbor) store was established in an old theater, and other locations included a former bank and [stock exchange](https://www.encyclopedia.com/social-sciences-and-law/economics-business-and-labor/money-banking-and-investment/stock-exchange). In 1993, Urban Outfitters stores averaged approximately 9,000 selling square feet.
The decor within each stores was also unique, although the atmosphere remained similar throughout the chain—casual and fun. Much of this was due to the staff and the company's policy of listening to its customers. Hayne hired staff within the targeted age group and depended on their personal style to guide merchandising strategies. Staff decided on the music to be played, even bringing in their own compact disks, and department managers were made responsible for the look of their sections. "We have to come up with creative inventions for fixtures and displays," housewares manager 27-year-old Susan Duckworth explained in the _Washington Post,_ adding that "It's the only place I've worked where you can bring an old crate to work, make something out of it and [the bosses] love it."

## Urban Outfitters Goes Public in 1993
Hayne used the capital to continue his strategic plan of growth by adding new stores on the retail side of the business and attracting new customers to the wholesale division while increasing sales to existing ones. In 1994, he opened three new Urban Outfitters stores, two in Chicago and one in Pasadena, and indicated that he planned to open three or four new stores each year for next three years, some of which were planned to be located outside the United States, either in Canada, [Europe](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/oceans-continents-and-polar-regions/oceans-and-continents/europe), or both. Based on the success of the Wayne, Pennsylvania, store, two more Anthropologie stores were opened in 1994, in Westport, Connecticut, and Rockville, [Maryland](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/united-states-and-canada/us-political-geography/maryland), just outside Washington, D.C. In the company's annual report that year, Hayne indicated he hoped to open three to four additional Anthropologie stores each year and that the company would invest heavily in expanding the Anthropologie division. Overall company sales grew by 30 percent from 1993. Recognizing that high rates of growth would be difficult to maintain, the company set a goal of 20 percent annual growth.
In 1995, an Urban Outfitters store opened in Portland, Oregon, and lease signings were announced in Austin, [Texas](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/united-states-and-canada/us-political-geography/texas), and Tempe, [Arizona](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/united-states-and-canada/us-political-geography/arizona), moving the company into the Southwest. With steadily increasing sales during this time, the company gained a ranking as number 76 on the _Business Week_ list of hot growth companies. As it neared the end of the 20th century, the Urban Outfitters and Anthropologie chains appeared to be going strong, and, after a quarter century, Hayne and his staff were still successfully anticipating and responding to shifts in fashion trends and the changing tastes of their customers.

## Urban Outfitters Goes Public in 1993
### Key Dates:
**1970:**Richard Hayne and Scott Belair open the first Free People Store.**1976:**Hayne moves to larger quarters, changes the store's name to Urban Outfitters, and incorporates the company.**1980:**A second store is opened in Massachusetts.**1984:**Hayne creates the wholesale division to design, produce, and sell its own line of junior sportswear.**1990:**The wholesale division replaces its signature Urban Outfitters collection brand with three separate labels: Ecote, Free People, and Anthropologie.**1992:**The first Anthropologie store opens.**1993:**The company goes public.**1998:**Urban Outfitters opens in London.**2002:**The first Free People retail store debuts.

## Late 1990s and Beyond
Urban Outfitters entered the late 1990s on solid ground. Despite having to close its first location near the [University of Pennsylvania](https://www.encyclopedia.com/social-sciences-and-law/education/colleges-us/university-pennsylvania) due to poor sales, the company forged ahead with is growth plans, buoyed by strong sales at its remaining outlets. In 1998, Anthropologie launched its direct-to-consumer catalog. Later that year, Urban Outfitters made its debut in London, opening its first store on Kensington High Street. During this period, Urban Outfitters' expansion was comparatively slower than many retail chains, however, despite the fact that it putting considerable effort into [market research](https://www.encyclopedia.com/social-sciences-and-law/economics-business-and-labor/economics-terms-and-concepts/market-research) before deciding to open a store. Company officials called each location a "complete lifestyle" store and were diligent in making sure it knew what its target customers wanted. Hayne explained the lifestyle label in a November 1998 _Retail Week_ article. "We have this concept where we have a unique and singular group of people that we are trying to service and we have a concept that emphasizes the lifestyle approach to servicing these customers. The product category to us is not particularly important, as long as we can make money, but the lifestyle is incredibly important."
Urban Outfitters continued its lifestyle strategy in the 2000s and experienced marked success. It expanded its store count while sales and profits increased. Fifteen stores were opened in 2000, 12 in 2001, and 15 in 2002. During 2003, approximately 20 Anthropologie stores opened their doors while 20 Urban Outfitters locations were added to the company's growing arsenal. The Urban Outfitters catalog was launched that year.

## Late 1990s and Beyond
The company opened its first Free People store in the Garden State Plaza Mall in Paramus, [New Jersey](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/united-states-and-canada/us-political-geography/new-jersey), in November 2002. A second location followed in December 2004 in Arlington, Virginia. During that year, Urban Outfitters was one of the most successful retailers, securing a revenue increase of nearly 50 percent while net income rose by 87 percent over the previous year.
With a solid financial record in place, Urban Outfitters planned to continue its expansion efforts in the coming years. Management hoped to increase store count by 20 percent per year, emphasizing that each location would continue to have its lifestyle focus. By 2005, there were over 75 Urban Outfitters stores in the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom. Over 65 Anthropologie stores accounted for nearly 39 percent of net sales in 2005. Its success in recent years left it in a enviable position among its competitors. Indeed, [Urban Outfitters Inc](https://www.encyclopedia.com/social-sciences-and-law/economics-business-and-labor/businesses-and-occupations/urban-outfitters). had a strong following, a solid strategy in place, and years of success under its belt. Hayne was confident that the company would remain a retail powerhouse well into the future.

#### Company History:
**Marciano Control Returns in Early 1990s**
The legal battle between the Marcianos and the Nakashes finally ended in early 1990, when a jury agreed with the Marcianos and returned 100 percent control of Guess to them. A second trial was set for May 1990 to determine damages. However, as the jury in that case was deliberating, the Marcianos announced that they had reached a settlement with the Nakashes for an undisclosed amount. This development occurred over the objections of their attorney, who pushed them to continue the case to full victory. The Marcianos stated, however, that they feared seeing the case continue through the appeals process and still more years of litigation. The Marcianos' attorney then sued them for $17 million in damages.
But with the battle with Jordache over, the Marcianos set about expanding their business. The years of litigation and the enormous attorneys' fees had limited their growth: the company believed that it would have topped $1 billion in sales by its tenth anniversary had it not been for the court case. With their resources freed up, the Marcianos increased their advertising budget to $22 million in 1991. The company also expanded its retail chain, to 33 stores by the end of 1991, including its European flagship store in Florence, Italy. While the recession of the early 1990s slowed growth somewhat, to 7 percent in 1991 compared to double-digits throughout the 1980s, Guess menswear took off, with a 41 percent sales growth in 1991 alone. By the end of that year, menswear accounted for just under 40 percent of company sales. International sales were also becoming more important to overall revenues. Licensing arrangements brought Guess [clothing](https://www.fundinguniverse.com/company-histories/guess-inc-history/#) to more than a dozen countries, with sales particularly strong in Canada and Japan.

#### Company History:
In 1993 Guess and its licensees registered an estimated $700 million in sales. In that year, Georges Marciano stepped down as the company's chairman, chief executive officer, and designer, citing differences of opinion with his brothers over the direction of the company. Georges, who had left the company briefly in 1988, sold his 40 percent share of the company to his brothers for an estimated $200 million. The year before, Maurice Marciano had also left the company, but he returned shortly before Georges Marciano's departure. Maurice was named chairman and chief executive officer and took over direction of design; Paul Marciano remained president and chief operating officer, and Armand continued to act as senior executive vice-president. After leaving Guess, Georges Marciano sued Guess and his brothers for allegedly infringing on the Georges Marciano trademark. Meanwhile, Georges opened a new company, Go USA Surfwear, and purchased 80 percent of Yes Clothing Company.
With Guess ads now featuring Maurice's name instead of Georges Marciano, Guess looked to its overhauled junior's line and international distribution, along with a stepped up promotional campaign, to fuel its further growth. Advertising spending reached $28 million in 1993; international sales were expected to reach 25 percent of total sales by the end of 1995. Licensing also continued to be an important source of revenue, with products now including home furnishings, infant wear, and junior knitwear. Sales of Guess watches topped $100 million in 1994, and Guess footwear sold more than $60 million. Meanwhile, Guess stores had also been growing, to an average of 3,500 square feet, and to 61 stores by the end of 1995, including a 7,000 square-foot store in Hawaii's Ala Moana Center and an 8,400 square-foot store in the Woodfield Mall in Schaumburg, Illinois. In less than fifteen years, the Guess label had grown from 30 pairs of [jeans](https://www.fundinguniverse.com/company-histories/guess-inc-history/#) to a diversified, billion-dollar branded empire.

**Competitive Pressures in Late 1990s**

#### Company History:
In 1996, Guess became a publicly traded company when it made its initial public offering in July. At about this same time, Guess continued with its earlier expansion plans. However, the next year was a disappointment to Guess due to weak performance in its [retail](https://www.fundinguniverse.com/company-histories/guess-inc-history/#) stores, weaknesses in its wholesale division, slower-than-expected non-core Asian licensing revenues, and discontinued licenses. However, three areas were stronger: its international operations, mostly in Latin America and Europe; certain core licensed product lines, such as handbags and accessories; and women's knitwear.
In 1998, Guess launched its new line of high-end ring-spun denim jeans called Premium Denim for both men and women. However, the company lost market share in 1998, mostly due to competitive pressures in the branded basic jeans business and a terrible retail environment. Guess started, in early 1999, its first virtual retail (e-commerce) store at its web site, http://www. Guess.com. The web site, since its inception, had consistent interactive success in combining fashion images, information, and technology.

Guess reduced its expansion plans in 2000 in order to concentrate more on improving investment returns, regaining business strength, and strengthening capital structure. Even so, Guess was still able to open 56 new stores in critical locations throughout the U.S. and Canada, while closing three under-performing stores. Guess also opened a new distribution facility in Louisville, Kentucky. In the fall, Guess introduced G Brand, a complete line of high-quality women's and men's jeanswear that used premium quality Italian ring spun denim in its European designs. Annual retail and wholesale sales increased by more than 32 percent. However, the company's profitability declined greatly because of higher retail occupancy costs due to less productive stores along with additional expenses for new stores; large inventories due to excessive buying and slowing sales trends; low productivity in its new Kentucky distribution facility; increased consulting fees; increased expenses with Guess Canada; and higher advertising expenses. At the end of 2000, Guess had 212 stores in the United States and Canada.

By 1995, Urban Outfitters stores would be established in Madison, [Wisconsin](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/united-states-and-canada/us-political-geography/wisconsin); [Ann Arbor](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/united-states-and-canada/us-political-geography/ann-arbor), [Michigan](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/united-states-and-canada/us-political-geography/michigan); Boston; [Minneapolis](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/united-states-and-canada/us-political-geography/minneapolis); [Seattle](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/united-states-and-canada/us-political-geography/seattle); [New York](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/united-states-and-canada/us-political-geography/new-york); Washington, D.C.; [Chicago](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/united-states-and-canada/us-political-geography/chicago); and Portland, Oregon. Moreover, the chain would also secure a presence in [California](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/united-states-and-canada/us-political-geography/california), with five locations in college towns. Even when Hayne was tempted to drift from his original concept, store locations kept the company focused on its college-age market.
texts.3:
## Beginnings
The new stores maintained Hayne's "counterculture" approach, and the company relied heavily on its buildings and interior displays to entice customers to enter, explore its stores, and buy its goods. "We always use renovated buildings," Hayne told the _Washington Post_ in a 1993 feature. "Other stores will go into a mall and put their image into a space, where we use an existing space to enhance our image. None of our stores look alike. We go into these old buildings and adapt them for ourselves," he noted. In Washington, D.C., for example, the company took over a Woolworth's store, complete with worn wooden floors, exposed brick walls, and a steel staircase to the basement. The [Ann Arbor](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/united-states-and-canada/us-political-geography/ann-arbor) store was established in an old theater, and other locations included a former bank and [stock exchange](https://www.encyclopedia.com/social-sciences-and-law/economics-business-and-labor/money-banking-and-investment/stock-exchange). In 1993, Urban Outfitters stores averaged approximately 9,000 selling square feet.
The decor within each stores was also unique, although the atmosphere remained similar throughout the chain—casual and fun. Much of this was due to the staff and the company's policy of listening to its customers. Hayne hired staff within the targeted age group and depended on their personal style to guide merchandising strategies. Staff decided on the music to be played, even bringing in their own compact disks, and department managers were made responsible for the look of their sections. "We have to come up with creative inventions for fixtures and displays," housewares manager 27-year-old Susan Duckworth explained in the _Washington Post,_ adding that "It's the only place I've worked where you can bring an old crate to work, make something out of it and [the bosses] love it."
texts.10:
## Urban Outfitters Goes Public in 1993
Hayne used the capital to continue his strategic plan of growth by adding new stores on the retail side of the business and attracting new customers to the wholesale division while increasing sales to existing ones. In 1994, he opened three new Urban Outfitters stores, two in Chicago and one in Pasadena, and indicated that he planned to open three or four new stores each year for next three years, some of which were planned to be located outside the United States, either in Canada, [Europe](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/oceans-continents-and-polar-regions/oceans-and-continents/europe), or both. Based on the success of the Wayne, Pennsylvania, store, two more Anthropologie stores were opened in 1994, in Westport, Connecticut, and Rockville, [Maryland](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/united-states-and-canada/us-political-geography/maryland), just outside Washington, D.C. In the company's annual report that year, Hayne indicated he hoped to open three to four additional Anthropologie stores each year and that the company would invest heavily in expanding the Anthropologie division. Overall company sales grew by 30 percent from 1993. Recognizing that high rates of growth would be difficult to maintain, the company set a goal of 20 percent annual growth.
In 1995, an Urban Outfitters store opened in Portland, Oregon, and lease signings were announced in Austin, [Texas](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/united-states-and-canada/us-political-geography/texas), and Tempe, [Arizona](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/united-states-and-canada/us-political-geography/arizona), moving the company into the Southwest. With steadily increasing sales during this time, the company gained a ranking as number 76 on the _Business Week_ list of hot growth companies. As it neared the end of the 20th century, the Urban Outfitters and Anthropologie chains appeared to be going strong, and, after a quarter century, Hayne and his staff were still successfully anticipating and responding to shifts in fashion trends and the changing tastes of their customers.

### Key Dates:
**1970:**Richard Hayne and Scott Belair open the first Free People Store.**1976:**Hayne moves to larger quarters, changes the store's name to Urban Outfitters, and incorporates the company.**1980:**A second store is opened in Massachusetts.**1984:**Hayne creates the wholesale division to design, produce, and sell its own line of junior sportswear.**1990:**The wholesale division replaces its signature Urban Outfitters collection brand with three separate labels: Ecote, Free People, and Anthropologie.**1992:**The first Anthropologie store opens.**1993:**The company goes public.**1998:**Urban Outfitters opens in London.**2002:**The first Free People retail store debuts.
texts.12:
## Late 1990s and Beyond
Urban Outfitters entered the late 1990s on solid ground. Despite having to close its first location near the [University of Pennsylvania](https://www.encyclopedia.com/social-sciences-and-law/education/colleges-us/university-pennsylvania) due to poor sales, the company forged ahead with is growth plans, buoyed by strong sales at its remaining outlets. In 1998, Anthropologie launched its direct-to-consumer catalog. Later that year, Urban Outfitters made its debut in London, opening its first store on Kensington High Street. During this period, Urban Outfitters' expansion was comparatively slower than many retail chains, however, despite the fact that it putting considerable effort into [market research](https://www.encyclopedia.com/social-sciences-and-law/economics-business-and-labor/economics-terms-and-concepts/market-research) before deciding to open a store. Company officials called each location a "complete lifestyle" store and were diligent in making sure it knew what its target customers wanted. Hayne explained the lifestyle label in a November 1998 _Retail Week_ article. "We have this concept where we have a unique and singular group of people that we are trying to service and we have a concept that emphasizes the lifestyle approach to servicing these customers. The product category to us is not particularly important, as long as we can make money, but the lifestyle is incredibly important."
Urban Outfitters continued its lifestyle strategy in the 2000s and experienced marked success. It expanded its store count while sales and profits increased. Fifteen stores were opened in 2000, 12 in 2001, and 15 in 2002. During 2003, approximately 20 Anthropologie stores opened their doors while 20 Urban Outfitters locations were added to the company's growing arsenal. The Urban Outfitters catalog was launched that year.
texts.13:
## Late 1990s and Beyond
The company opened its first Free People store in the Garden State Plaza Mall in Paramus, [New Jersey](https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/united-states-and-canada/us-political-geography/new-jersey), in November 2002. A second location followed in December 2004 in Arlington, Virginia. During that year, Urban Outfitters was one of the most successful retailers, securing a revenue increase of nearly 50 percent while net income rose by 87 percent over the previous year.
With a solid financial record in place, Urban Outfitters planned to continue its expansion efforts in the coming years. Management hoped to increase store count by 20 percent per year, emphasizing that each location would continue to have its lifestyle focus. By 2005, there were over 75 Urban Outfitters stores in the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom. Over 65 Anthropologie stores accounted for nearly 39 percent of net sales in 2005. Its success in recent years left it in a enviable position among its competitors. Indeed, [Urban Outfitters Inc](https://www.encyclopedia.com/social-sciences-and-law/economics-business-and-labor/businesses-and-occupations/urban-outfitters). had a strong following, a solid strategy in place, and years of success under its belt. Hayne was confident that the company would remain a retail powerhouse well into the future.

**AND1** is an American footwear and clothing company specializing in [basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball "Basketball") shoes, clothing, and sporting goods. AND1 was founded on August 13, 1993. The company focuses strictly on basketball and is a subsidiary of Galaxy Universal.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-galax-1)
The company sponsors [NBA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA "NBA") athletes, as well as numerous high school and AAU teams in the United States.

In 1993, AND1 began as a graduate school project [partnership](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partnership "Partnership") of Jay Coen Gilbert, Seth Berger, and Tom Austin while they were graduate students at the [University of Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Pennsylvania "University of Pennsylvania")'s [Wharton School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wharton_School "Wharton School").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:042-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:1-3) The company name is derived from a phrase used by [basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball "Basketball")[broadcasters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_presenter "Sports presenter") to denote a [free throw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_throw "Free throw") awarded to a player against whom a foul has been committed while scoring a goal.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:44-4)

The brand started by selling T-shirts out of the back of a car.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:32-5) Early advertising strategies included other basketball [slogans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slogans "Slogans") and [trash talk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trash_talk "Trash talk"), such as "Pass. Save Yourself The Embarrassment".[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-chicago-sports-review3-6) They targeted the niche market of street basketball players and avoided branching out to other markets.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-7)[Foot Locker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foot_Locker "Foot Locker") began to sell the shirts, and within the second year of launching, the business reached 1,500 stores across America.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:042-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:1-3) The company's first big endorsee was [Larry Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Johnson_(basketball,_born_1969) "Larry Johnson (basketball, born 1969)"), who briefly wore their shirts.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:44-4)

In 1996, NBA star [Stephon Marbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephon_Marbury "Stephon Marbury") became the first spokesman for AND1.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:042-2) That year, the company released its first basketball sneakers.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:32-5) That same year, AND1 signed [Raef LaFrentz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raef_LaFrentz "Raef LaFrentz") and [Larry Hughes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Hughes "Larry Hughes").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-Souphanh-9) From 1997 to 1998, AND1 quadrupled its market share.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:32-5)
[![Image 2](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f3/Taichissw.jpg/250px-Taichissw.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Taichissw.jpg)
A pair of AND1 basketball shoes

### The Skip Tape and success
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=AND1&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: The Skip Tape and success")]
In 1994, a [videotape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Videotape "Videotape") containing [streetball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streetball "Streetball") stunts was delivered to AND1 by Marquise Kelly, coach of the [Benjamin Cardozo High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_N._Cardozo_High_School "Benjamin N. Cardozo High School") team in [Queens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queens "Queens"), [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)"). The tape contained low-quality video, poor resolution, and nearly indecipherable audio featuring a [streetballer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streetballer "Streetballer") named [Rafer Alston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rafer_Alston "Rafer Alston").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-wbur/and1-mixtapes2-10) This tape sat on a shelf until 1998, when it was edited and used at events. At the time, Alston was a student at [Fresno State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_State_University,_Fresno "California State University, Fresno") who had entered the [1998 NBA draft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_NBA_draft "1998 NBA draft").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:542-11) The videotape would soon be known as the "Skip tape", referring to Alston's streetball nickname "Skip to my Lou".[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-Original_AND1_Mixtape2-12) Alston later signed on with AND1.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:222-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-14)

### The Skip Tape and success
In 1999 at [Haverford College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haverford_College "Haverford College") in [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia"), AND1 shot its first series of [commercials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercials "Commercials") and [print ads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Print_ad "Print ad")[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:042-2) incorporating [NBA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA "NBA") players [Darrell Armstrong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darrell_Armstrong "Darrell Armstrong"), [Rex Chapman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rex_Chapman "Rex Chapman"), Ab Osondu, [Raef LaFrentz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raef_LaFrentz "Raef LaFrentz"), [Toby Bailey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toby_Bailey "Toby Bailey"), and [Miles Simon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Simon "Miles Simon").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:542-11) The company signed [Latrell Sprewell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latrell_Sprewell "Latrell Sprewell") in 1999.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:32-5) His shoe, the AND1 Spree, was released in 2002.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-15) When the traditional marketing campaign proved unsuccessful, a strategy was formed to use the Skip tape. It was edited and reprinted into 50,000 copies, and over the next eight weeks, distributed across basketball camps, clinics, and record labels.

### The Skip Tape and success
The tape would become the first "[Mixtape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_mixtape "Video mixtape")", and quickly made Alston into a celebrity.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:542-11)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:222-13)
When AND1 became a product partner with [FootAction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foot_Locker "Foot Locker"), this strategy evolved into a national program.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:44-4)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:542-11) Starting in the summer of 1999, a free AND1 Mixtape was given with any purchase. Approximately 200,000 tapes were distributed in the span of three weeks.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-chicago-sports-review3-6)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:222-13)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:62-16) It proved to be so successful that the company put together a team of streetball legends to serve as a traveling team and filmed new mixtapes.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:542-11) By the end of the year, the Philadelphia-based company had more than 70 employees.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:44-4)
[![Image 3](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e6/And1_basketball_shoes.jpg/250px-And1_basketball_shoes.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:And1_basketball_shoes.jpg)
AND1 basketball shoes

### The Skip Tape and success
AND1 gained fame when [Vince Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vince_Carter "Vince Carter") won the 2000 [Slam Dunk Contest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slam_Dunk_Contest "Slam Dunk Contest") while wearing its Tai Chi shoes.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-Souphanh-9)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-17) He was then featured on the cover of the April 2000 issue of [Slam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slam_(magazine) "Slam (magazine)") wearing another pair.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-18) The company went on to sell more than a million shoes.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-19) By the 2001 season, AND1 was second only to Nike in market share and had $285 million in revenue.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:042-2) The company also signed [Kevin Garnett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Garnett "Kevin Garnett") and [Jamal Crawford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamal_Crawford "Jamal Crawford").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-21)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:1-3)

### The Skip Tape and success
In 2002, the AND1 summer tours were expanded into the Mixtape Tour. "Open runs" were also introduced, where local street ballers were given a chance to go up against AND1's team. The best from that group would join the summer tour and receive endorsement deals from AND1. [Grayson Boucher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grayson_Boucher "Grayson Boucher"), aka "The Professor," was the first to win a spot on the team.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-chicago-sports-review3-6)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:542-11)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:2-22) Founder Tom Austin left the company in 2003.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:042-2) Another iconic moment for the brand came in 2004, when [Chauncey Billups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chauncey_Billups "Chauncey Billups") won the [NBA Finals MVP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_Finals_Most_Valuable_Player "NBA Finals Most Valuable Player") while wearing the AND1 Rise sneaker.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-23)

### The Skip Tape and success
By 2005, AND1 had 165 employees, $180 million in annual revenue, and sold its products in 125 countries. That May, it was announced that AND1 had been acquired by American Sporting Goods, which also owned brands like [Avia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avia_(shoes) "Avia (shoes)"), [Ryka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryk%C3%A4 "Rykä"), Nevados, Yukon, Turntec, NSS, and Apex.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:542-11)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-24) Berger and Gilbert left soon after the sale.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:042-2)
In February 2011, ASG was purchased by [Brown Shoe Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caleres "Caleres"). By this time, Avia, Ryka, and AND1 made up 80% of the group's sales.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-25) Brown quickly divested AND1, selling the brand to the newly-formed Galaxy Brands in August 2011.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-26) In November 2012, AND1 signed then-[Pacer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana_Pacers "Indiana Pacers")[Lance Stephenson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lance_Stephenson "Lance Stephenson") to an endorsement deal.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-27) The company also signed 2013 rookies [Isaiah Canaan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaiah_Canaan "Isaiah Canaan") and [Jamaal Franklin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamaal_Franklin "Jamaal Franklin").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-28)

AND1 **began its journey in 1993** when Jay Coen Gilbert, Seth Berger, and Tom Austin started a t-shirt company out of the trunk of a car **while studying at the University of Pennsylvania**. The t-shirts featured the legendary faceless hooper and different trash talk phrases typically heard on the blacktops across America. In the mid-1990s, AND1 was chugging along as just another basketball brand. That is, until a fateful day in 1998.**A tape was delivered to AND1** containing blurry, homemade streetball footage by a high school basketball coach from Queens, New York. The tape featured a spectacular New York City point guard by the name of [**Rafer Alston, aka Skip To My Lou**](https://www.basketball-reference.com/players/a/alstora01.html). Having an “aka” was about to get wildly popular. And the videotape would soon be known as the **“Skip Tape”**.

Early in 1999, after a failed traditional marketing campaign, AND1 decided to use the “Skip tape” as a marketing tool and reprinted **50,000 copies**. Over the next eight weeks, it was distributed to basketball camps, clinics, and record labels. The tape would become the first basketball mixtape, and quickly made Alston an underground celebrity.

## **AND1: Origins**
In the **summer of 1999**, AND1 created a clever marketing strategy that would prove pivotal to the brand. A free highlight tape was given to everyone who purchased AND1 products. The tape was known [**as the AND1 Mixtape**](https://and1.com/pages/and1-reels?utm_source=organic&utm_medium=weartesters&utm_campaign=thirty-years). Approximately **200,000 tapes were distributed in three weeks**, making this promotion one of the most successful in U.S. retail history.
The **effects of this tape were felt in the NBA** and in the basketball world for over a decade as a generation of players copied and introduced this new school of streetball into the zeitgeist. The success of AND1 had the basketball shoe market on their heels scrambling to ride the streetball wave.
**EA Sports released the NBA and NFL street video games** series (some of the most fun games ever made, in my opinion). Nike put out their battleground product line and video series, while the NBA released the NBA street, ankle breakers, and dunk DVD series. The born-to-ball DVD was even a thing. It wasn’t the best era for technical basketball, but damn, it was fun.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GI4ilfUnNsw&ab_channel=RyanVanDusen
With our hearts filled with nostalgia, we present our top ten list of AND1 basketball shoes.

**AND1** is an American footwear and clothing company specializing in [basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball "Basketball") shoes, clothing, and sporting goods. AND1 was founded on August 13, 1993. The company focuses strictly on basketball and is a subsidiary of Galaxy Universal.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-galax-1)
The company sponsors [NBA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA "NBA") athletes, as well as numerous high school and AAU teams in the United States.

In 1993, AND1 began as a graduate school project [partnership](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partnership "Partnership") of Jay Coen Gilbert, Seth Berger, and Tom Austin while they were graduate students at the [University of Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Pennsylvania "University of Pennsylvania")'s [Wharton School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wharton_School "Wharton School").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:042-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:1-3) The company name is derived from a phrase used by [basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball "Basketball")[broadcasters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_presenter "Sports presenter") to denote a [free throw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_throw "Free throw") awarded to a player against whom a foul has been committed while scoring a goal.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:44-4)

The brand started by selling T-shirts out of the back of a car.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:32-5) Early advertising strategies included other basketball [slogans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slogans "Slogans") and [trash talk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trash_talk "Trash talk"), such as "Pass. Save Yourself The Embarrassment".[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-chicago-sports-review3-6) They targeted the niche market of street basketball players and avoided branching out to other markets.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-7)[Foot Locker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foot_Locker "Foot Locker") began to sell the shirts, and within the second year of launching, the business reached 1,500 stores across America.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:042-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:1-3) The company's first big endorsee was [Larry Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Johnson_(basketball,_born_1969) "Larry Johnson (basketball, born 1969)"), who briefly wore their shirts.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:44-4)

In 1996, NBA star [Stephon Marbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephon_Marbury "Stephon Marbury") became the first spokesman for AND1.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:042-2) That year, the company released its first basketball sneakers.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:32-5) That same year, AND1 signed [Raef LaFrentz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raef_LaFrentz "Raef LaFrentz") and [Larry Hughes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Hughes "Larry Hughes").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-Souphanh-9) From 1997 to 1998, AND1 quadrupled its market share.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:32-5)
[![Image 2](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f3/Taichissw.jpg/250px-Taichissw.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Taichissw.jpg)
A pair of AND1 basketball shoes

### The Skip Tape and success
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=AND1&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: The Skip Tape and success")]
In 1994, a [videotape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Videotape "Videotape") containing [streetball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streetball "Streetball") stunts was delivered to AND1 by Marquise Kelly, coach of the [Benjamin Cardozo High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_N._Cardozo_High_School "Benjamin N. Cardozo High School") team in [Queens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queens "Queens"), [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)"). The tape contained low-quality video, poor resolution, and nearly indecipherable audio featuring a [streetballer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streetballer "Streetballer") named [Rafer Alston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rafer_Alston "Rafer Alston").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-wbur/and1-mixtapes2-10) This tape sat on a shelf until 1998, when it was edited and used at events. At the time, Alston was a student at [Fresno State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_State_University,_Fresno "California State University, Fresno") who had entered the [1998 NBA draft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_NBA_draft "1998 NBA draft").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:542-11) The videotape would soon be known as the "Skip tape", referring to Alston's streetball nickname "Skip to my Lou".[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-Original_AND1_Mixtape2-12) Alston later signed on with AND1.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:222-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-14)

### The Skip Tape and success
Paying homage to Brooklyn streetball culture, AND1 partnered with _[SLAM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slam\_(magazine) "Slam (magazine)")_ magazine to host numerous events surrounding the [2015 NBA All-Star Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_NBA_All-Star_Game "2015 NBA All-Star Game"), played at the [Barclays Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barclays_Center "Barclays Center") in [downtown Brooklyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_Brooklyn "Downtown Brooklyn"). Various charity events with two of New York's greatest streetball legends Lance Stephenson and [Rafer "Skip to My Lou" Alston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rafer_Alston "Rafer Alston") were followed by the launch of an exclusive pop-up retail lounge on Flatbush Avenue across from Barclays Center.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-IR222-31)
In July 2016, AND1 signed [Brooklyn Nets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Nets "Brooklyn Nets") guard [Sean Kilpatrick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Kilpatrick "Sean Kilpatrick").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-32) Over one hundred AND1 High School and AAU teams play across America in various tournaments and leagues, and an AND1 circuit in the making.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-35) In 2017, the brand introduced its own youth basketball circuit under the Dominate the Game name.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-37)

### The Skip Tape and success
Looking to re-establish itself in the market, AND1 announced in 2018 that Kevin Garnett would serve Creative Director and Global Ambassador.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-38) It also named [Jevon Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jevon_Carter "Jevon Carter") and Thomas Beauchamp as ambassadors.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-39) In 2019, AND1 signed [Toronto Raptors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto_Raptors "Toronto Raptors") point guard [Fred VanVleet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_VanVleet "Fred VanVleet") to a major sponsorship deal and helped introduce the company's Action 2.0 shoe.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-40)[Montrezl Harrell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montrezl_Harrell "Montrezl Harrell") also briefly signed on before the deal fell through, though he continued to wear AND1 shoes.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-41) In 2021, the company signed VanVleet's teammate [Norman Powell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Powell "Norman Powell").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-42)

### The Skip Tape and success
On August 31, 2021, Sequential Brands, AND1's parent, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-43) In September 2021, AND1 was acquired by Galaxy Universal.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-galax-1)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-45) In 2022, AND1 was featured in the [Netflix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix "Netflix") documentary [Untold: The Rise and Fall of And1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Untold:_The_Rise_and_Fall_of_AND1 "Untold: The Rise and Fall of AND1") from director [Kevin Wilson Jr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Wilson_Jr. "Kevin Wilson Jr.").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:042-2)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-46) For its 30th anniversary in 2023, AND1 reintroduced its open run events in order to foster a new generation of streetball.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:62-16)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-47) In 2024, the company released a short documentary on the career of [Ben Wallace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Wallace_(basketball) "Ben Wallace (basketball)").[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-49) It also introduced [Alexis Morris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexis_Morris "Alexis Morris") as its first female ambassador.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-50)

AND1's summer tours began in 1999. The original group included Half Man Half Amazing, Shane the Dribble Machine, [Main Event](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waliyy_Dixon "Waliyy Dixon"), Aircraft, [Future](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malloy_Nesmith_Sr. "Malloy Nesmith Sr."), and Headache.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:44-4) In 2002, the tour was expanded into the [AND1 Mixtape Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1_Mixtape_Tour "AND1 Mixtape Tour"), featuring [streetball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streetball "Streetball") players of fame.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-chicago-sports-review3-6) Other standouts were [Skip to My Lou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rafer_Alston "Rafer Alston"), [The Professor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grayson_Boucher "Grayson Boucher"), [Hot Sauce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Champion "Philip Champion"), [Spyda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dennis_Chism "Dennis Chism"), 50, and [AO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Owens "Aaron Owens").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:2-22)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:7-51)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-52) From 2002 to 2008, the tours were televised live on ESPN under the name “Streetball”[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:542-11) and competed with ESPN's [SportsCenter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SportsCenter "SportsCenter") for the highest ratings.

**AND1** is an American footwear and clothing company specializing in [basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball "Basketball") shoes, clothing, and sporting goods. AND1 was founded on August 13, 1993. The company focuses strictly on basketball and is a subsidiary of Galaxy Universal.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-galax-1)
The company sponsors [NBA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA "NBA") athletes, as well as numerous high school and AAU teams in the United States.
texts.1: In 1993, AND1 began as a graduate school project [partnership](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partnership "Partnership") of Jay Coen Gilbert, Seth Berger, and Tom Austin while they were graduate students at the [University of Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Pennsylvania "University of Pennsylvania")'s [Wharton School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wharton_School "Wharton School").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:042-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:1-3) The company name is derived from a phrase used by [basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball "Basketball")[broadcasters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_presenter "Sports presenter") to denote a [free throw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_throw "Free throw") awarded to a player against whom a foul has been committed while scoring a goal.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:44-4)
texts.2: The brand started by selling T-shirts out of the back of a car.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:32-5) Early advertising strategies included other basketball [slogans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slogans "Slogans") and [trash talk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trash_talk "Trash talk"), such as "Pass. Save Yourself The Embarrassment".[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-chicago-sports-review3-6) They targeted the niche market of street basketball players and avoided branching out to other markets.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-7)[Foot Locker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foot_Locker "Foot Locker") began to sell the shirts, and within the second year of launching, the business reached 1,500 stores across America.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:042-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:1-3) The company's first big endorsee was [Larry Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Johnson_(basketball,_born_1969) "Larry Johnson (basketball, born 1969)"), who briefly wore their shirts.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:44-4)
texts.3:
In 1996, NBA star [Stephon Marbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephon_Marbury "Stephon Marbury") became the first spokesman for AND1.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:042-2) That year, the company released its first basketball sneakers.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:32-5) That same year, AND1 signed [Raef LaFrentz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raef_LaFrentz "Raef LaFrentz") and [Larry Hughes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Hughes "Larry Hughes").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-Souphanh-9) From 1997 to 1998, AND1 quadrupled its market share.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:32-5)

### The Skip Tape and success
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=AND1&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: The Skip Tape and success")]
In 1994, a [videotape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Videotape "Videotape") containing [streetball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streetball "Streetball") stunts was delivered to AND1 by Marquise Kelly, coach of the [Benjamin Cardozo High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_N._Cardozo_High_School "Benjamin N. Cardozo High School") team in [Queens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queens "Queens"), [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)"). The tape contained low-quality video, poor resolution, and nearly indecipherable audio featuring a [streetballer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streetballer "Streetballer") named [Rafer Alston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rafer_Alston "Rafer Alston").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-wbur/and1-mixtapes2-10) This tape sat on a shelf until 1998, when it was edited and used at events. At the time, Alston was a student at [Fresno State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_State_University,_Fresno "California State University, Fresno") who had entered the [1998 NBA draft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_NBA_draft "1998 NBA draft").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:542-11) The videotape would soon be known as the "Skip tape", referring to Alston's streetball nickname "Skip to my Lou".[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-Original_AND1_Mixtape2-12) Alston later signed on with AND1.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:222-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-14)
texts.11:
### The Skip Tape and success
Paying homage to Brooklyn streetball culture, AND1 partnered with _[SLAM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slam\_(magazine) "Slam (magazine)")_ magazine to host numerous events surrounding the [2015 NBA All-Star Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_NBA_All-Star_Game "2015 NBA All-Star Game"), played at the [Barclays Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barclays_Center "Barclays Center") in [downtown Brooklyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_Brooklyn "Downtown Brooklyn"). Various charity events with two of New York's greatest streetball legends Lance Stephenson and [Rafer "Skip to My Lou" Alston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rafer_Alston "Rafer Alston") were followed by the launch of an exclusive pop-up retail lounge on Flatbush Avenue across from Barclays Center.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-IR222-31)
In July 2016, AND1 signed [Brooklyn Nets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Nets "Brooklyn Nets") guard [Sean Kilpatrick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Kilpatrick "Sean Kilpatrick").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-32) Over one hundred AND1 High School and AAU teams play across America in various tournaments and leagues, and an AND1 circuit in the making.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-35) In 2017, the brand introduced its own youth basketball circuit under the Dominate the Game name.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-37)
texts.12:
### The Skip Tape and success
Looking to re-establish itself in the market, AND1 announced in 2018 that Kevin Garnett would serve Creative Director and Global Ambassador.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-38) It also named [Jevon Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jevon_Carter "Jevon Carter") and Thomas Beauchamp as ambassadors.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-39) In 2019, AND1 signed [Toronto Raptors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto_Raptors "Toronto Raptors") point guard [Fred VanVleet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_VanVleet "Fred VanVleet") to a major sponsorship deal and helped introduce the company's Action 2.0 shoe.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-40)[Montrezl Harrell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montrezl_Harrell "Montrezl Harrell") also briefly signed on before the deal fell through, though he continued to wear AND1 shoes.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-41) In 2021, the company signed VanVleet's teammate [Norman Powell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Powell "Norman Powell").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-42)
texts.13:
### The Skip Tape and success
On August 31, 2021, Sequential Brands, AND1's parent, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-43) In September 2021, AND1 was acquired by Galaxy Universal.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-galax-1)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-45) In 2022, AND1 was featured in the [Netflix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix "Netflix") documentary [Untold: The Rise and Fall of And1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Untold:_The_Rise_and_Fall_of_AND1 "Untold: The Rise and Fall of AND1") from director [Kevin Wilson Jr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Wilson_Jr. "Kevin Wilson Jr.").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:042-2)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-46) For its 30th anniversary in 2023, AND1 reintroduced its open run events in order to foster a new generation of streetball.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:62-16)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-47) In 2024, the company released a short documentary on the career of [Ben Wallace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Wallace_(basketball) "Ben Wallace (basketball)").[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-49) It also introduced [Alexis Morris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexis_Morris "Alexis Morris") as its first female ambassador.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-50)

### The Skip Tape and success
AND1's summer tours began in 1999. The original group included Half Man Half Amazing, Shane the Dribble Machine, [Main Event](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waliyy_Dixon "Waliyy Dixon"), Aircraft, [Future](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malloy_Nesmith_Sr. "Malloy Nesmith Sr."), and Headache.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:44-4) In 2002, the tour was expanded into the [AND1 Mixtape Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1_Mixtape_Tour "AND1 Mixtape Tour"), featuring [streetball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streetball "Streetball") players of fame.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-chicago-sports-review3-6) Other standouts were [Skip to My Lou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rafer_Alston "Rafer Alston"), [The Professor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grayson_Boucher "Grayson Boucher"), [Hot Sauce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Champion "Philip Champion"), [Spyda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dennis_Chism "Dennis Chism"), 50, and [AO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Owens "Aaron Owens").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:2-22)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:7-51)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-52) From 2002 to 2008, the tours were televised live on ESPN under the name “Streetball”[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AND1#cite_note-:542-11) and competed with ESPN's [SportsCenter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SportsCenter "SportsCenter") for the highest ratings.
